usage: the route or space you cover takes 을/를, not 에
걷다 pairs naturally with speed adverbs 천천히·빨리
걸어서 = 'by walking', the standard way to say 'on foot'
duration uses 동안; the walking distance itself can drop the particle
examples: 저는 매일 공원을 걸어요.
I walk in the park every day.
걷다 is intransitive but the park you traverse takes 을 as the path
역까지 걸어서 십 분 걸려요.
It takes ten minutes on foot to the station.
걸어서 'on foot' is the everyday answer to how you get somewhere
다리를 다쳐서 지금은 잘 못 걸어요.
I hurt my leg, so I can't walk well right now.
못 걸어요 uses the ㄷ→ㄹ vowel form; 못 걷어요 is wrong
nuance: 걷다 means to walk on foot and is a ㄷ irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ softens to ㄹ, so the 요-form is 걸어요 (not 걷어요) and the past is 걸었어요. Before a consonant ending the ㄷ stays put, so the formal form remains 걷습니다 and you say 걷지 마세요, 걷고 싶어요. The nearest relative is 산책하다 ('take a stroll'): 걷다 is the raw act of walking anywhere, while 산책하다 implies a leisurely walk for pleasure, so 'I walk to work' is 걸어서 출근해요, never 산책해서 출근해요. The trap for English speakers is that 걷다 doesn't take an object the way 'walk the dog' does — Korean uses 산책시키다 for that, and the path you walk takes 을/를 (공원을 걸어요), so don't reach for 에. Also remember 걸어서 ('on foot') is one fixed chunk for describing how you travel.

Translating 'walk the dog' literally as 개를 걸어요 — 걷다 can't take a creature as its object that way; Korean says 개를 산책시켜요 ('make the dog stroll').

usage: 뛰다 pairs with speed adverbs 빨리·열심히
직역 'rush toward' — 뛰다 covers dashing, not just sport
same verb means 'jump'; 제자리 = in place
the standard sign/warning in stations and hallways
examples: 아이들이 운동장에서 뛰어요.
The kids run around the playground.
everyday running/dashing about, not timed sport
지각할까 봐 역까지 뛰었어요.
I ran to the station because I was afraid of being late.
뛰다 = rushing to make it on time
여기는 병원이니까 뛰지 마세요.
This is a hospital, so please don't run.
뛰지 마세요 keeps ㅁ before the consonant ending
nuance: 뛰다 is a regular verb whose stem ends in the vowel 위, so it simply adds 어 without contracting: 뛰어요, 뛰었어요. Before the formal ㅂ/ㄴ endings the stem shortens in the usual way to 뜁니다 and 뛸 거예요. Its key synonym is 달리다: 달리다 is the neutral, 'sporty' word for running over distance (마라톤을 달리다, 100미터를 달리다), while 뛰다 is the everyday word for dashing, rushing, or even jumping, so a child rushing across a room 뛰어다녀요 rather than 달려다녀요. Crucially 뛰다 also means 'to jump/leap' (제자리에서 뛰다 = jump in place; 심장이 뛰다 = the heart beats/pounds), so context decides between 'run' and 'jump'. The English-speaker pitfall is spelling: don't confuse 뛰다 (run) with 띄다 ('be visible / catch the eye', as in 눈에 띄다) — they sound close but are different verbs. Also note the polite-warning 뛰지 마세요 is the fixed phrase you'll see posted everywhere.

Assuming 뛰다 only means timed/sport running and switching to 달리다 for a quick dash — for rushing to catch a bus or train, natural Korean is 버스를 타려고 뛰었어요, not 달렸어요.
Forgetting the stem-shortening in the formal form and saying 뛰읍니다 — the correct formal present is 뜁니다 (and the future is 뛸 거예요).

usage: the spot where you stand takes 에 (여기에), often dropped in speech
I line up / stand in line
fixed collocation 줄(을) 서다 = 'form a line'
for vehicles 서다 = come to a stop
서다 pairs with posture adverbs 똑바로·가만히
examples: 문 앞에 서 주세요.
Please stand in front of the door.
place + 에 marks where you take your standing position
사람들이 길게 줄을 섰어요.
People formed a long line.
줄을 서다 is the set phrase for queuing; 섰어요 is the contracted past
택시가 우리 앞에 갑자기 섰어요.
The taxi suddenly stopped in front of us.
same verb = a vehicle coming to a halt
nuance: 서다 means to stand or, for vehicles, to come to a stop. Because the stem already ends in 어, the 요-ending merges instead of doubling: you get 서요 and the past 섰어요, never 서어요 or 서었어요. Watch the two sister verbs: 서다 is the plain state/result 'to be standing / take a standing position', while 일어서다 ('rise to one's feet') stresses the motion of getting up from sitting — so 'please stand up (from your seat)' is 일어서 주세요, but 'please stand here' is 여기 서 주세요. For vehicles 서다 overlaps with 멈추다 ('to halt'); 멈추다 is more general and can describe machines or actions stopping, while 서다 is the everyday word for a bus or car pulling up. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the location where you stand takes 에 (여기에 서다), not the object marker, and don't say 줄에 서다 — the idiom is 줄을 서다, treating the line as something you 'do'. Korean also has no separate verb for 'stand something up'; that meaning needs the causative 세우다.

usage: I lie down on the bed
surface you lie on takes 에
I lie down for a bit
눕다 pairs with 잠깐·좀 for a short rest
posture adverbs 똑바로·옆으로 go with 눕다
누워서 + verb = doing something while lying down
examples: 저는 침대에 누워요.
I lie down on the bed.
the bed (place) takes 에; 누워요 is the ㅂ→우 vowel form
너무 피곤해서 소파에 누웠어요.
I was so tired that I lay on the sofa.
누웠어요 keeps the 우 from the irregular stem
여기 잠깐 누워 보세요.
Please lie down here for a moment.
누워 보세요 = 'try lying down', a gentle suggestion
nuance: 눕다 means to lie down and is a ㅂ irregular verb: before a vowel ending the ㅂ turns into a 우/워 sound, giving 누워요 and 누웠어요, while before a consonant the ㅂ stays, so the formal is 눕습니다 and you say 눕지 마세요, 눕고 싶어요. Don't confuse it with two neighbors: 눕다 is intransitive ('I lie down'), whereas the causative 눕히다 means 'lay someone/something down' (아기를 눕혀요 = lay the baby down), and 기대다 means 'to lean/recline' rather than fully lying flat. There's also a posture pair to keep straight: 눕다 (lie) vs 앉다 (sit) vs 서다 (stand). The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'lie down' has no object but learners still want to add 를; in Korean the surface takes 에 (침대에 눕다), and reaching for 눕어요 by analogy with regular verbs is the classic error — it must be 누워요.

usage: what you lift or carry takes 을/를
fixed phrase 손(을) 들다 = raise one's hand
the everyday way to ask someone to carry something briefly
examples: 이 가방 좀 들어 주세요.
Please hold this bag for me.
좀 + 들어 주세요 softens the request
혼자서 무거운 상자를 들었어요.
I lifted the heavy box by myself.
들었어요 keeps the ㄹ before a vowel
질문이 있으면 손을 드세요.
If you have a question, raise your hand.
드세요 — the ㄹ drops before the honorific 세요
nuance: 들다 here means to lift or hold something up in your hand, and it is a ㄹ irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before endings beginning with ㅂ, ㄴ, or ㅅ, so you get 듭니다, 드세요, and 드는 — but the ㄹ stays before a plain vowel, giving 들어요 and 들었어요. Note the future is simply 들 거예요 (the ㄹ survives before ㄱ). Its near-synonym 올리다 means 'to raise/put up' and stresses upward movement to a higher place (가격을 올리다 = raise the price), while 들다 is about taking the weight in your hand or holding it, and 나르다 (also ㄹ-irregular: 날라요) means 'transport/haul' over a distance. Beware: 들다 is a famously overloaded verb — it also means 'to enter' (방에 들다), 'to cost/take' (돈이 들다, 시간이 들다), and 'to like the taste' in 마음에 들다. The English-speaker pitfall is conjugation: by analogy with regular verbs people write 들읍니다, but the ㄹ must drop, so it's 듭니다; and 'raise your hand' is 손을 들다, not 손을 올리다.

usage: what you set down takes 을/를
the spot where you place it takes 에
I let go / release my grip
놓다 also = 'let go of', 손을 놓다
Please put it down / let go
놔 주세요 is the natural contracted form in speech
examples: 가방을 의자에 놓았어요.
I put the bag on the chair.
object + 를, place + 에: the basic 놓다 pattern
컵을 여기에 놓아 주세요.
Please put the cup here.
놓아 주세요 = a polite request to set something down
뜨거우니까 그 냄비 그냥 놓으세요.
It's hot, so just put that pot down.
놓으세요 with 으 before the honorific after a consonant stem
nuance: 놓다 means to set an object down onto a surface, and the place where you put it takes 에 (책상에 놓다 = put it on the desk). It's a regular verb, so the ㅎ stays in writing and you add 아: 놓아요, 놓았어요; in fast speech 놓아요 routinely contracts to 놔요 and 놓았어요 to 놨어요, but the full forms are clearer to learn first. The crucial contrast is with 넣다 ('put inside / insert'): 놓다 places something ON a surface, while 넣다 puts it INTO a container (가방에 넣다 = put it in the bag) — choosing the wrong one changes the meaning entirely. Compare too 두다 ('leave/keep something in a place', often longer-term: 여기 두세요 = leave it here). 놓다 also means 'to let go / release' (손을 놓다) and appears in helpful patterns like -아 놓다 ('do and leave it done', 켜 놓다 = leave it switched on). The English-speaker pitfall: English 'put' covers both 'on' and 'in', so learners overuse 놓다 where 넣다 is needed, and they mark the surface with 를 instead of the correct 에.

usage: garments worn on the torso/legs take 을/를 with 입다
옷(을) 입다 is the generic 'get dressed'
uniforms and formal wear use 입다
입어 보다 = 'try on (clothing)' in a shop
examples: 오늘은 따뜻한 옷을 입어요.
Today I'm wearing warm clothes.
weather-driven clothing choice; 옷을 입다 generic
친구 결혼식이라서 정장을 입었어요.
I wore a suit because it was a friend's wedding
정장 ('formal suit') is what you wear for special occasions
이 코트 한번 입어 보세요.
Try this coat on.
입어 보세요 is what a shop clerk says
nuance: 입다 is a regular verb (입어요, 입었어요, 입습니다) meaning to put on or wear clothing on the torso and legs — shirts, coats, dresses, trousers, uniforms. The thing English speakers must internalize is that Korean has no single verb for 'wear'; it splits the action by body part: 입다 for body clothes, 신다 for footwear (shoes, socks), 쓰다 for things on the head/face (hats, glasses), 끼다 for snug items (gloves, rings), 차다 for things you strap on (watch, belt), and 매다 for ties/scarves you knot. So 'wear shoes' is never 신발을 입다 — it must be 신발을 신다. A second nuance is aspect: 입다 is the action of putting on, while the resulting state 'be wearing' is 입고 있다 (티셔츠를 입고 있어요 = is wearing a T-shirt). The opposite, for taking off any of these, is the single verb 벗다. The pitfall is simply over-extending 입다 to cover everything 'wear' covers in English.

Saying 옷을 입고 있어요 when you mean the action of getting dressed right now — 입고 있다 is ambiguous toward the state 'am wearing'; to stress the ongoing action of dressing, context or 입는 중이에요 is clearer.

usage: 벗다 covers footwear too, unlike the put-on side
Come in after taking off your shoes
벗고 + verb sequences the action; common at the door
examples: 집에서는 신발을 벗어요.
At home we take off our shoes.
Korean custom; 신발을 벗다 even though putting on is 신다
너무 더워서 외투를 벗었어요.
It was so hot that I took off my coat.
벗었어요 regular past
실내에서는 모자를 벗어 주세요.
Please take off your hat indoors.
벗어 주세요 polite request
nuance: 벗다 is the single, regular verb (벗어요, 벗었어요, 벗습니다) for taking off almost anything you wear — clothes, shoes, socks, a hat, glasses, gloves. This is the great convenience of Korean: the 'put on' side fragments into 입다/신다/쓰다/끼다/차다 by body part, but the 'take off' side collapses into just 벗다, so you don't have to match the item to a special remover. (Two small exceptions: accessories you fasten — a watch, a ring, a tie — are usually 풀다 'undo/untie' or 빼다 'pull out', so 시계를 풀다, 반지를 빼다 sound more natural than 벗다.) The everyday context is the Korean custom of removing shoes at the door: 신발을 벗고 들어오세요. The English-speaker pitfall is over-thinking it: learners who learned that shoes need 신다 sometimes invent a matching remover, but for taking off you simply use 벗다 for clothes, shoes, and hats alike. Don't say 안 신어요 to mean 'take off shoes' — that just means 'don't wear shoes'.

usage: body parts you wash take 을/를
씻다 fits hands, face, and food
rinsing food with water uses 씻다
examples: 밥 먹기 전에 손을 씻어요.
I wash my hands before eating.
habit; 손을 씻다 fixed collocation
저는 아침마다 찬물로 얼굴을 씻어요.
I wash my face with cold water every morning.
with-instrument 찬물로; 씻어요 regular
딸기를 흐르는 물에 깨끗이 씻으세요.

The whole-body version is 씻다 generically, or the Sino-Korean 샤워하다 'shower'. examples: 저는 보통 운동화를 신어요.

운동화를 신다; 신어요 regular

양말을 신다 — socks use 신다, not 입다

So 'wear sneakers' must be 운동화를 신다 and 'put on socks' is 양말을 신다 — using 입다 here is a clear error a native speaker would immediately notice. The matching state 'have on / be wearing' is 신고 있다 (장화를 신고 있어요 = is wearing boots), and the opposite is the all-purpose 벗다 (신발을 벗다). The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 입다 for everything wearable; remember the foot-specific 신다 and that socks, not just shoes, belong to it.

usage: 웃다 pairs with size adverbs 크게·활짝
활짝 웃다 = beam/grin; 웃다 covers smiling too
the standard phrase when taking a photo

웃었어요 regular past; 크게 웃다 collocation
아기가 저를 보고 활짝 웃어요.
The baby smiles brightly at me.
보고 웃다 = smile at (seeing); 웃다 = smile here

The near-synonym 미소(를) 짓다 ('make a smile', literally) is more written/formal and only means smiling, whereas plain 웃다 is the everyday word for both. A related verb to keep distinct is the causative 웃기다 ('to be funny / make someone laugh', 웃기다 ≠ 웃다): 그 사람 진짜 웃겨요 = 'that person is really funny'. Naturally its opposite is 울다 ('to cry'). usage: the crier is the subject and takes 이/가
울고 싶다 expresses the urge to cry
examples: 아기가 밤에 자주 울어요.
The baby often cries at night.
subject 아기가; 울어요 keeps ㄹ before a vowel
슬픈 영화를 보고 펑펑 울었어요.
I sobbed watching a sad movie.
펑펑 울다 intensifies; 울었어요 past
울지 마세요, 다 괜찮아질 거예요.

nuance: 울다 means to cry and is a ㄹ irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before endings starting with ㅂ, ㄴ, or ㅅ, so the formal present is 웁니다 (not 울습니다) and the honorific is 우세요; before a plain vowel the ㄹ stays, giving 울어요 and 울었어요, and the future keeps it too in 울 거예요. The crier is the subject and takes 이/가 (아기가 울어요), unlike English where 'cry' can feel transitive. Its natural opposite is 웃다 (laugh), and its near-synonyms split by intensity and register: 눈물을 흘리다 ('shed tears', literally, more composed/quiet) describes tears running down without sobbing, while 흐느끼다 ('to sob') is heavier and more literary; plain 울다 is the everyday all-purpose word, often boosted by mimetics like 펑펑 울다 (bawl) or 엉엉 울다. Note 울다 also describes animals making their cry/call (새가 울다 = a bird sings/cries) and even a phone or alarm 'ringing/sounding'. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation — writing 울습니다 by habit when the ㄹ must drop to 웁니다 — plus confusing 울다 with 웃다, which differ by a single jamo.
